title: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The core of human thinking is based on rather simple rules

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Despite the complicated construction of the brain, there is a core to human thinking that is largely independent of neural details and is based on rather simple rules, with nothing fundamentally special about the processes involved.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I strongly suspect that there is a definite core to the phenomenon of human thinking that is largely independent of such details—and that will in the end turn out to be based on rules that are rather simple.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Human Thinking” (from p. 620), p. 628. Scope: human thinking and its emulation by artificial systems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-21: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.32

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Specific compact cognitive architectures can be benchmarked, but their success would not show that they capture the unique core of human thinking. The claim lacks a discriminating consequence against more complex or implementation-dependent accounts.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Without quantitative definitions of the cognitive core, independence from neural details, rule simplicity, and what would count as fundamentally special, behavioral equivalence cannot confirm or refute the statement.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Core and simplicity are undefined.

Multiple implementations can fit the same behavior.

The claim combines empirical and metaphysical assertions.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.25

discriminating power: 0.2

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is that thinking has a core of simple rules largely independent of how neurons are built. Brain and behavior datasets record the neural detail and some performance, but they do not contain that core or a test of its implementation independence. Deciding the claim needs an explicit rule-level account that has not been produced.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Specify a small rule set claimed to be the core of thinking, show that its behavior is unchanged under changes of neural implementation, and compare it with human performance. A core that survives implementation changes and matches behavior would support the claim; essential dependence on particular neural detail would refute independence.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'Rather simple rules' and 'a definite core' are not tied to a stated formal system.

Existing brain maps record neural detail; they do not contain a demonstration that thinking is independent of it.
